items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "context collapse".
items.answer: The merging of different audiences (family, friends, employers) into one online audience, making self-presentation harder (Marwick and boyd, 2011)

items.stem: Explain why foundational digital ID systems can both include and exclude people.
items.answer: They let people without paper documents access welfare, banking and SIM cards, but if biometric authentication fails (worn fingerprints, poor connectivity) or enrolment is hard, people can be denied services they are entitled to.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: They let people without paper documents access welfare, banking and SIM cards, but if biometric authentication fails (worn fingerprints, poor connectivity) or enrolment is hard, people can be denied services they are entitled to. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Ingrid writes: "Aadhaar is mandatory for every service in India, including private bank accounts." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: In Puttaswamy (2018) the Supreme Court upheld Aadhaar for welfare and tax (PAN linking) but struck down Section 57, so private companies cannot make it mandatory, e.g. for bank accounts or mobile SIMs.
items.markingKey: In Puttaswamy (2018) the Supreme Court upheld Aadhaar for welfare and tax (PAN linking) but struck down Section 57, so private companies cannot make it mandatory, e.g. for bank accounts or mobile SIMs. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Read the source below.

"On the Internet, nobody knows you're a dog."
— Caption of a cartoon by Peter Steiner, The New Yorker (1993)

Explain what the source suggests about identity online and how this has changed since 1993.
items.answer: It suggested the early internet allowed anonymity and freely chosen identities; today tracking, real-name policies, data profiling and digital ID mean platforms often know a great deal about who users are.
items.markingKey: It suggested the early internet allowed anonymity and freely chosen identities; today tracking, real-name policies, data profiling and digital ID mean platforms often know a great deal about who users are. Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem: With reference to context collapse on social media, explain how it illustrates self-presentation online.
items.answer: Researchers Marwick and boyd (2011) showed that Twitter users imagine audiences and self-censor because friends, family and employers see the same posts. When audiences merge, users must craft a single identity acceptable to all, changing how people express who they are.
items.markingKey: Context (Researchers Marwick and boyd (2011) showed that Twitter users imagine audiences and self-censor because friends, family and employers see the same posts.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: when audiences merge, users must craft a single identity acceptable to all, changing how people express who they are. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to self-presentation online.

items.stem: Alessia writes: "Your digital identity consists only of what you choose to post." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Digital identity also includes data others post about you and passive data trails (location, browsing, purchases) collected and inferred by companies.
items.markingKey: Digital identity also includes data others post about you and passive data trails (location, browsing, purchases) collected and inferred by companies. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "A single national digital ID does more good than harm."
items.answer: Digital ID can bring major benefits when backed by strong privacy law, offline alternatives and independent oversight; without them, harms can outweigh gains for the most vulnerable.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: inclusion of people without documents (Aadhaar); efficient, less corrupt delivery of welfare and services (Estonia). Arguments against: exclusion through authentication failures; privacy and surveillance risks from centralised databases; function creep into areas beyond the original purpose. Supported judgement: Digital ID can bring major benefits when backed by strong privacy law, offline alternatives and independent oversight; without them, harms can outweigh gains for the most vulnerable.

items.stem: Compare how a social-media profile and a government digital ID shape a person's identity, and evaluate which has the greater impact on their life chances.
items.answer: Compare self-presented vs assigned identity, control, audiences and consequences (e.g. Instagram vs Aadhaar/e-ID); evaluate impact on access to services, jobs and rights; support with examples.

items.stem: Explain why people may present different identities on different platforms.

items.stem: Explain why anonymity online can be both protective and harmful.
items.answer: Anonymity protects whistle-blowers, activists and LGBTQ+ people from persecution, but it can also reduce accountability and enable harassment, trolling and fraud.

items.stem: Distinguish between a legal digital identity and a social (self-presented) identity.
items.answer: A social identity is how a person chooses to present themselves online (profiles, posts); a legal digital identity is an official credential that proves who they are (e.g. Aadhaar, e-ID).
items.markingKey: A social identity is how a person chooses to present themselves online (profiles, posts); a legal digital identity is an official credential that proves who they are (e.g. Aadhaar, e-ID). items.stem: With reference to Estonia's e-ID and e-Residency, explain how it illustrates digital identity as access to services and citizenship.
items.answer: Estonian citizens use a chip-based ID card or Smart-ID to vote online, sign documents and access almost all public services; e-Residency (2014) extends a digital identity to foreigners. Identity becomes a key to the state's digital services, enabling efficiency and remote participation, but concentrating trust in one system (a 2017 chip vulnerability forced certificate updates).
items.markingKey: Context (Estonian citizens use a chip-based ID card or Smart-ID to vote online, sign documents and access almost all public services; e-Residency (2014) extends a digital identity to foreigners.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.stem: With reference to two real-world examples, discuss the claim that people have more freedom to choose their identity online than offline.
items.answer: Online spaces offer new freedom to explore identity, but platforms and data systems also define and constrain identity in ways users do not control.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: avatars, pseudonyms and communities allow exploration of identity; LGBTQ+ youth can find support anonymously. items.stem: With reference to Epic Games v. Apple, explain how it illustrates gatekeeping power.
items.answer: Apple removed Fortnite from the App Store in 2020 after Epic introduced direct payments; a 2021 US ruling required Apple to allow links to outside payments, and the EU DMA later required alternative app stores in the EU. Apple's control of the only app store on iPhones let it set commissions and rules, and the case shows how courts and regulators try to limit that power.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "Large technology platforms now have more power than many governments."
items.answer: Platforms hold distinctive infrastructural and discursive power that rivals small states, but governments with large markets and strong laws can still constrain them.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: they control communication infrastructure for billions of people; they can deplatform leaders and set global rules; their revenues exceed the GDP of many states. Arguments against: states can still legislate, fine and ban (EU fines, Nigeria's Twitter ban, China's control of platforms); platforms lack armies and taxation powers; states can force data localisation and takedowns. Supported judgement: Platforms hold distinctive infrastructural and discursive power that rivals small states, but governments with large markets and strong laws can still constrain them.

items.answer: In January 2021 Apple and Google removed the Parler app from their stores and Amazon Web Services stopped hosting it, taking it offline for weeks. items.stem: "Regulation such as the EU Digital Markets Act can effectively limit platform power." How far do you agree? Refer to at least one Digital Society concept in your answer.
items.answer: The DMA can shift some power, especially over app stores and self-preferencing, but its effect depends on enforcement and on whether competitors and users actually switch.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: large fines (up to 10% of global turnover) and specific obligations (alternative app stores, interoperability); the EU market is too large to ignore (Brussels effect). Arguments against: gatekeepers comply minimally or appeal; enforcement is slow and complex; network effects may keep users on dominant platforms anyway. Supported judgement: The DMA can shift some power, especially over app stores and self-preferencing, but its effect depends on enforcement and on whether competitors and users actually switch. items.answer: Users have some responsibility, but because platforms design and profit from engagement, they and regulators (e.g. design codes, the DSA) carry the greater responsibility.

items.stem: With reference to two real-world examples, discuss the claim that a single national digital ID does more good than harm.
items.answer: Digital ID can bring major benefits when backed by strong privacy law, offline alternatives and independent oversight; without them, harms can outweigh gains for the most vulnerable.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: inclusion of people without documents (Aadhaar); efficient, less corrupt delivery of welfare and services (Estonia). Arguments against: exclusion through authentication failures; privacy and surveillance risks from centralised databases; function creep into areas beyond the original purpose. Supported judgement: Digital ID can bring major benefits when backed by strong privacy law, offline alternatives and independent oversight; without them, harms can outweigh gains for the most vulnerable. items.stem: "Regulation such as the EU Digital Markets Act can effectively limit platform power." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: The DMA can shift some power, especially over app stores and self-preferencing, but its effect depends on enforcement and on whether competitors and users actually switch.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: large fines (up to 10% of global turnover) and specific obligations (alternative app stores, interoperability); the EU market is too large to ignore (Brussels effect). Arguments against: gatekeepers comply minimally or appeal; enforcement is slow and complex; network effects may keep users on dominant platforms anyway. Supported judgement: The DMA can shift some power, especially over app stores and self-preferencing, but its effect depends on enforcement and on whether competitors and users actually switch. items.stem: Which biometric data are collected for Aadhaar enrolment?
options: Fingerprints, iris scans and a facial photograph
Handwriting samples
DNA samples
Voice recordings only
items.answer: Fingerprints, iris scans and a facial photograph
items.markingKey: A. Aadhaar uses ten fingerprints, both irises and a photograph.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "digital resistance"?
options: The merging of different audiences (family, friends, employers) into one online audience, making self-presentation harder (Marwick and boyd, 2011)
Using digital tools such as hashtags, petitions, crowdfunding and livestreams to campaign for social or political change
Actions by users or groups that challenge or evade the power of platforms or states, such as encryption, VPNs, boycotts or hacktivism
A government-issued digital identity used to prove who a person is across many services, such as India's Aadhaar or Estonia's e-ID
items.answer: Actions by users or groups that challenge or evade the power of platforms or states, such as encryption, VPNs, boycotts or hacktivism
items.markingKey: C. "digital resistance" is actions by users or groups that challenge or evade the power of platforms or states, such as encryption, VPNs, boycotts or hacktivism.

items.stem: Who wrote that "a wealth of information creates a poverty of attention" (1971)?
items.answer: Herbert Simon
items.markingKey: Herbert Simon. Simon's observation is the origin of the attention economy idea.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a social (self-presented) identity and a legal digital identity.
items.answer: A social identity is how a person chooses to present themselves online (profiles, posts); a legal digital identity is an official credential that proves who they are (e.g. Aadhaar, e-ID).
items.markingKey: A social identity is how a person chooses to present themselves online (profiles, posts); a legal digital identity is an official credential that proves who they are (e.g. Aadhaar, e-ID). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student claims: "Platforms are neutral spaces that simply host content." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Platforms make design and ranking choices, set rules and monetise attention, so they actively shape what users see and do.
items.markingKey: Platforms make design and ranking choices, set rules and monetise attention, so they actively shape what users see and do. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A student claims: "Hashtag campaigns never lead to real-world change." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Some do: #MeToo contributed to investigations, resignations and law changes; #BlackLivesMatter organised protests and policy debates; online awareness can support offline action.
items.markingKey: Some do: #MeToo contributed to investigations, resignations and law changes; #BlackLivesMatter organised protests and policy debates; online awareness can support offline action. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between pseudonymity and anonymity.
items.answer: Anonymity means no stable identifier links actions to a person; pseudonymity uses a consistent alias that builds a reputation without revealing the legal name.
items.markingKey: Anonymity means no stable identifier links actions to a person; pseudonymity uses a consistent alias that builds a reputation without revealing the legal name. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why network effects give large platforms power.
items.answer: Each new user makes the platform more valuable to others (more friends, sellers, buyers), so users stay even if they dislike its rules; rivals struggle to attract users, letting the dominant platform set terms for users, advertisers and businesses.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Each new user makes the platform more valuable to others (more friends, sellers, buyers), so users stay even if they dislike its rules; rivals struggle to attract users, letting the dominant platform set terms for users, advertisers and businesses. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between a user as a customer and a user as the product in the attention economy.
items.answer: A customer pays for a service; in the attention economy free services are funded by selling users' attention and data to advertisers, so the user's attention is effectively what is sold.
items.markingKey: A customer pays for a service; in the attention economy free services are funded by selling users' attention and data to advertisers, so the user's attention is effectively what is sold. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student claims: "Your digital identity consists only of what you choose to post." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Digital identity also includes data others post about you and passive data trails (location, browsing, purchases) collected and inferred by companies.
items.markingKey: Digital identity also includes data others post about you and passive data trails (location, browsing, purchases) collected and inferred by companies. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Read the source below.

"If you want to reach iPhone users, there is only one door, and Apple holds the key and charges for entry."
— Statement by an app developer at a 2021 hearing on app-store competition

With reference to the source, explain how Apple exercises power over developers.
items.answer: Apple controls the only route (the App Store) to iPhone users, so developers must accept its rules and commission; this is gatekeeping power based on control of access.
items.markingKey: Apple controls the only route (the App Store) to iPhone users, so developers must accept its rules and commission; this is gatekeeping power based on control of access. Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem: With reference to autoplay and infinite scroll, explain how it illustrates the attention economy.
items.answer: Aza Raskin, who designed infinite scroll in 2006, later said he regretted how it was used to keep people scrolling. A design choice that removes stopping cues increases time on platforms, which converts attention into advertising revenue.
items.markingKey: Context (Aza Raskin, who designed infinite scroll in 2006, later said he regretted how it was used to keep people scrolling.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: a design choice that removes stopping cues increases time on platforms, which converts attention into advertising revenue. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the attention economy.

items.stem: Using Estonia's e-ID and e-Residency as an example, explain digital identity as access to services and citizenship.
items.answer: Estonian citizens use a chip-based ID card or Smart-ID to vote online, sign documents and access almost all public services; e-Residency (2014) extends a digital identity to foreigners. Identity becomes a key to the state's digital services, enabling efficiency and remote participation, but concentrating trust in one system (a 2017 chip vulnerability forced certificate updates).

items.stem: Using Epic Games v. Apple as an example, explain gatekeeping power.
items.answer: Apple removed Fortnite from the App Store in 2020 after Epic introduced direct payments; a 2021 US ruling required Apple to allow links to outside payments, and the EU DMA later required alternative app stores in the EU. Apple's control of the only app store on iPhones let it set commissions and rules, and the case shows how courts and regulators try to limit that power.

items.stem: Briefly describe #MeToo (2017) and explain what it reveals about online activism.
items.answer: After allegations against Harvey Weinstein, Alyssa Milano invited women to reply "me too"; the hashtag was used millions of times in many countries. A simple hashtag made the scale of sexual harassment visible and connected survivors globally, contributing to resignations, prosecutions and workplace policy changes.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Large technology platforms now have more power than many governments."
items.answer: Platforms hold distinctive infrastructural and discursive power that rivals small states, but governments with large markets and strong laws can still constrain them.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: they control communication infrastructure for billions of people; they can deplatform leaders and set global rules; their revenues exceed the GDP of many states. Arguments against: states can still legislate, fine and ban (EU fines, Nigeria's Twitter ban, China's control of platforms); platforms lack armies and taxation powers; states can force data localisation and takedowns. Supported judgement: Platforms hold distinctive infrastructural and discursive power that rivals small states, but governments with large markets and strong laws can still constrain them.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "People have more freedom to choose their identity online than offline."
items.answer: Online spaces offer new freedom to explore identity, but platforms and data systems also define and constrain identity in ways users do not control.
